What the filter does real librealsense SDK, not a reimplementation

Numpy depth frames decoded from the bag are injected into a rs.software_device — a synthetic sensor the compiled pyrealsense2 SDK will accept frames from — so Intel's own spatial, temporal, and hole-filling filters process this data exactly as they would a live D455's stream. RGB is not involved in this stage; librealsense's post-processing filters are depth-only. (RGB is used earlier, in the pixel-matching/alignment stage that produced this bag's aligned-depth topic in the first place.)

Processing order per frame

raw uint16 depth→ range gate [0.30, 6.00]m→ depth→disparity→ spatial filter→ temporal filter→ disparity→depth→ hole filling

Disparity-domain processing (rather than filtering metric depth directly) is Intel's own design: stereo depth noise grows roughly with the square of range, so smoothing behaves more uniformly across near/far pixels in disparity space. The temporal filter is stateful — one filter instance is reused for all 2,678 frames in order; a fresh instance per frame would silently disable cross-frame persistence.

Parameters used "aggressive," as requested

ParameterRangeUsedWhy
spatial_magnitude1–55Max iterations — single-frame only, no motion risk.
spatial_smooth_alpha0.25–1.00.25Minimum — maximum smoothing weight toward neighbors.
spatial_smooth_delta1–5050Max edge tolerance in disparity levels.
spatial_holes_fill0–53Spatial filter's own light local hole extrapolation.
temporal_smooth_alpha0–10.20Near-min, not min — Go1 is moving; full temporal weight risks smearing real scene changes, not just noise.
temporal_smooth_delta1–10040Same moving-platform caveat.
temporal_holes_fill0–85Persistency mode for cross-frame hole recovery.
hole_fill_mode0–22nearest_from_around — extends foreground into gaps rather than background (library default is 1/farthest).
min/max_depth_m—0.30 / 6.00Wide on purpose — the runtime pipeline already gates to 0.30–4.0m three times downstream; this bake stays permissive.

Roughness: did smoothing actually smooth? a more careful look

Local roughness is measured as |value − median of its neighborhood|, averaged only over pixels whose entire neighborhood was valid (never contaminated by a hole edge). Measured at two scales — 3×3 (pixel-to-pixel dither) and 9×9 (coarser waviness) — and in three populations: real measurements before filtering, the identical pixel locations after filtering, and territory that hole-filling invented from nothing.

WindowBefore (real)After, same pixelsChangeHole-filled territory
3×3 (fine)0.42 mm1.14 mm+171%9.33 mm
9×9 (coarse)0.37 mm4.00 mm+992%31.69 mm
Honest reading of this number: roughness on already-good pixels increased at both scales, and more so at the coarser one. 3×3 roughness rose from 0.42 mm to 1.14 mm (+171%); 9×9 roughness rose from 0.37 mm to 4.00 mm (+992%) — proportionally the larger jump, which rules out "fine dither only" as the full story. The most likely mechanism: every parameter pushed to its most aggressive setting (§2) is an edge-preserving filter with a hard threshold (spatial_smooth_delta, temporal_smooth_delta) gating which neighbors get blended. At maximum aggressiveness this is known to trade smooth gradients for piecewise-flat "plateaus" — individually low-roughness at 3×3, but stepping between adjacent plateaus shows up as elevated roughness at a window wide enough to span more than one of them, which is exactly what a 9×9 window is more likely to do than a 3×3 one. In absolute terms this is still small: the coarse-scale increase (4.00 mm) is about 6× smaller than the 2.28 cm mean (and roughly 45× smaller than the 18.10 cm max) the filter is actually revising already-valid pixels by — so real corrective smoothing at a coarser scale is still the dominant effect, this is a secondary one riding on top of it. It does not reverse the headline result (coverage 72.0% → 97.1%), but it is a real, concrete cost of choosing the most aggressive setting on every parameter rather than a moderate one, and worth weighing if smooth large-scale geometry matters more than maximum coverage for a given use of this bag. A natural follow-up (not run here) would repeat this same before/after analysis with each filter parameter at its library default instead of its extreme, to see where the coverage/roughness trade-off actually bends.

Separately, and expectedly, roughness inside hole-filled territory is higher still (9.33 mm at 3×3, 31.69 mm at 9×9) than either real-measurement population — that territory is extrapolated, not sensed, and nearest_from_around fill can create patchwork seams at the boundaries of what it fills.

Caveats

Depth-only. This filter stage does not use RGB. It runs the same post-processing a live D455 would run on its own depth stream. RGB's role in this bag is upstream, in pixel-matching depth to the rectified color grid.

No ground truth. All metrics here are internal consistency checks (coverage, self-agreement, local smoothness) — there is no independent, higher-accuracy depth reference for this bag to compute true error against.

Temporal settings were deliberately not maxed for the moving-platform reason in §2's parameter table; a stationary-sensor recording could likely push temporal smoothing further without the same motion-smearing risk.

A separate, unrelated finding surfaced while tracing topics for this pipeline: rsg_pipeline_go1.yaml's rgb: key points at the raw (distorted) color topic while depth is aligned to the rectified geometry — a real geometric mismatch, but orthogonal to this filtering experiment and not yet fixed as of this report.
